title: Common Causes of Female Infertility: What Every Woman Should Know
excerpt: Age, ovulation, blocked tubes, endometriosis and sperm quality: the common causes, and what each test actually tells you.

body.text: Every woman’s fertility journey is different. For some couples, pregnancy happens within a few months. For others, it may take longer, even when they are doing everything right. When conception is delayed, the first step is not to blame yourself. The first step is to understand what may be happening in the body.

Female infertility can have many causes. Some are related to ovulation, some to the fallopian tubes or uterus, and some to hormones, age, lifestyle or underlying medical conditions. In a few couples, all basic reports may appear normal, and the reason may not be immediately clear.

If you are trying to conceive and looking for guidance on female infertility or fertility treatment in Chennai, understanding the possible causes can help you ask the right questions and seek care at the right time.
Medical note: This article is for educational purposes only. It is not a substitute for consultation with a qualified gynecologist or fertility specialist.
What Does Female Infertility Mean?

Pregnancy depends on several steps working together. An egg must be released from the ovary, sperm must reach the egg, fertilisation must occur, and the fertilised egg must travel to the uterus and implant in the uterine lining. If any one of these steps is affected, pregnancy may take longer than expected.

In general, a fertility evaluation is advised when a couple has been having regular unprotected intercourse for over 06 months without pregnancy. If the woman is 35 years or older, it is better to seek evaluation after six months of trying. Women above 40, or women with known concerns such as irregular periods, very painful periods, PCOS, endometriosis, previous pelvic infection, pelvic surgery or repeated pregnancy loss, should consider speaking to a specialist earlier.

A fertility consultation does not automatically mean IVF. Often, the first step is simply to understand ovulation, hormone levels, the uterus, fallopian tubes and semen parameters, so that the couple receives advice suited to their situation.
1. Irregular Ovulation

Ovulation is the release of an egg from the ovary. If ovulation does not happen regularly, the chances of pregnancy in a given cycle can reduce. This is one of the most common causes of female infertility.
Signs that ovulation may be irregular include: Periods that come very late or are frequently missed
Cycles that vary widely from month to month Long gaps between periods Very light or unpredictable bleeding patterns
2. PCOS
Polycystic Ovary Syndrome, commonly called PCOS, is a hormonal condition that can affect menstrual cycles and ovulation. It is common, but it does not affect every woman in the same way.
Women with PCOS may have: Irregular or delayed periods Acne or oily skin Increased facial or body hair

Weight gain or difficulty losing weight Irregular ovulation Having PCOS does not mean that a woman cannot become pregnant. Many women with PCOS conceive naturally, while some may need treatment to improve ovulation or address associated metabolic or hormonal issues. The treatment plan depends on age, cycle pattern, ultrasound findings, hormone profile, weight, medical history and how long the couple has been trying.
3. Blocked or Damaged Fallopian Tubes

The fallopian tubes are the pathways where the egg and sperm usually meet. After ovulation, the egg enters the fallopian tube, and sperm travels upward to meet it. If one or both tubes are blocked or damaged, fertilisation may become difficult.

Tubal blockage may occur after pelvic infections, sexually transmitted infections, pelvic inflammatory disease, endometriosis, previous abdominal or pelvic surgery, or a past ectopic pregnancy. Many women with blocked tubes do not have obvious symptoms, which is why tubal assessment may be recommended during fertility evaluation.

Tests such as HSG or similar imaging procedures can help assess whether the fallopian tubes are open. The next step depends on whether one tube or both tubes are affected, the woman’s age, other fertility factors and the couple’s overall plan.
4.Endometriosis
Some discomfort during periods is common, but severe pain that affects school, college, work, sleep or daily routine should not be ignored. One possible cause of severe period pain is endometriosis.

Endometriosis occurs when tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows outside the uterus. It may involve the ovaries, fallopian tubes, pelvic lining or surrounding structures. In some women, it can affect egg quality, ovulation, tubal function, pelvic anatomy or implantation.
Symptoms may include:

items: Painful bowel movements or urinary symptoms during periods

body.text: Endometriosis varies widely from person to person. Some women have severe symptoms with mild disease, while others may have advanced disease with fewer symptoms. If pain is persistent or fertility is delayed, a gynecologist or fertility specialist can guide the appropriate evaluation and treatment options.
5. Age-Related Fertility Changes

Age is an important factor in female fertility. Women are born with a fixed number of eggs. With time, both the number and quality of eggs gradually decline. This change becomes more significant in the mid-to-late 30s and especially after 40.

This does not mean that pregnancy after 35 is impossible. Many women have healthy pregnancies after 35. However, it is useful to understand that the time available to evaluate and treat fertility concerns becomes shorter with age. Early consultation helps couples make informed decisions rather than waiting without clarity.
For women who are planning pregnancy later, fertility awareness, ovarian reserve testing when appropriate, and discussion of options such as fertility preservation may be helpful.
6. Hormonal Problems

Hormones regulate the menstrual cycle, ovulation and preparation of the uterus for pregnancy. Thyroid disorders, high prolactin levels and other endocrine conditions can interfere with ovulation or cycle regularity.

Symptoms such as sudden cycle changes, missed periods, unusually heavy bleeding, breast discharge, unexplained weight changes, fatigue, excess hair growth or acne may suggest a hormonal contribution. Simple blood tests often help identify these issues, and many hormonal problems can be managed effectively once diagnosed.
7. Conditions Affecting the Uterus
The uterus is where the embryo implants and pregnancy grows. Certain uterine conditions can make it more difficult for pregnancy to begin or continue.
These may include: Fibroids, especially those that distort the uterine cavity Endometrial polyps
Scar tissue inside the uterus Congenital differences in the shape of the uterus Thin or irregular endometrial lining in selected cases

Not every fibroid or uterine finding affects fertility. The significance depends on size, location, symptoms, ultrasound findings and fertility history. A specialist can help decide whether treatment is needed or whether observation is sufficient.
8. Lifestyle and General Health Factors
Lifestyle is only one part of fertility, and fertility problems should never be reduced to blame or guilt. Still, general health can influence reproductive health.

Smoking, excessive alcohol intake, significantly low or high body weight, poor sleep, uncontrolled diabetes, untreated thyroid disease and certain medications can affect fertility in some women. A balanced diet, regular physical activity, adequate sleep and management of existing medical conditions can support overall health and fertility treatment outcomes.
At the same time, lifestyle changes cannot correct every fertility issue. If pregnancy is delayed, medical evaluation is important rather than relying only on diet, rest or stress reduction.
9. Unexplained Infertility

Sometimes, the reports look reassuring: ovulation appears normal, fallopian tubes are open, the uterus looks healthy and semen parameters are acceptable. Yet pregnancy does not happen. This is called unexplained infertility.

The term can feel frustrating, but it does not mean that there is no hope. It simply means that the available tests have not identified one clear cause. Depending on age, duration of infertility, previous treatments and test results, options may include expectant management for a limited time, ovulation induction, IUI or IVF.
When Should You See a Fertility Specialist?
It may be time to consult a fertility specialist if:

items: You have been trying to conceive for over 06 months without success
You are 35 or older and have been trying for six months
You are above 40 and planning pregnancy
Your periods are very irregular or frequently missed
You have PCOS, endometriosis or known fibroids
You have had pelvic infection, pelvic surgery or ectopic pregnancy
You have had two or more miscarriages
You simply want to understand your fertility before planning pregnancy

body.text: A good fertility evaluation usually looks at both partners. Even when the concern appears to be female infertility, semen analysis is an important part of assessment because fertility depends on egg, sperm, tubes, uterus and timing working together.
Can Female Infertility Be Treated?

In many cases, yes. The right treatment depends on the underlying cause. One woman may need correction of a thyroid or prolactin problem. Another may need ovulation support. Someone else may benefit from treatment for endometriosis, fibroids or tubal disease. Some couples may need IUI or IVF.

There is no single treatment that is right for every woman. Age, medical history, scan findings, hormone reports, ovarian reserve, semen analysis and the duration of infertility all influence the plan. This is why personalised evaluation is important.
Do Not Blame Yourself

When pregnancy takes longer than expected, women often receive advice from every direction: relax, stop thinking about it, eat a particular food, take a holiday, reduce stress. Most of this advice is well meant, but it can unintentionally make a woman feel responsible for something that may have a medical cause.

Difficulty conceiving does not make anyone less healthy, less feminine or less deserving of motherhood. Asking for help is not a failure. It is a sensible step toward understanding the body and choosing the right way forward.
Listen to Your Body

Your menstrual cycle, pain pattern, hormone symptoms and overall health can give important clues. If your periods are very irregular, if pain is severe, if you have PCOS or endometriosis, or if you have been trying to conceive without success, you do not have to wait for years in uncertainty.

Sometimes the first step is not treatment. Sometimes the first step is simply finding the reason. Once the reason is understood, your doctor can explain the options and help you decide what is appropriate for your body, your age and your plans.

title: Sperm DNA fragmentation index
excerpt: A normal semen analysis does not rule out sperm DNA damage. What the fragmentation index measures, and when we test for it.

body.text: Semen analysis and sperm DNA fragmentation testing represent fundamental diagnostic tools in the evaluation of male fertility. While semen analysis quantitatively assesses parameters such as sperm concentration, motility, and morphology, it does not provide insight into sperm functional quality. The DNA Fragmentation Index (DFI) complements semen analysis by detecting underlying sperm DNA damage, thereby offering valuable qualitative assessment that may contribute to infertility.

What is DNA Fragmentation index? The DNA Fragmentation Index (DFI) provides a quantitative measure of DNA fragmentation and damage within the sperm head (1). In healthy sperm, DNA is highly compacted to protect the genetic material that conveys hereditary information from parent to offspring. However, sperm DNA can become exposed and damaged due to various internal and external factors such as oxidative stress, defective germ cell development, apoptosis, heat exposure, environmental pollutants, and unhealthy lifestyle habits (e.g., smoking, poor diet, obesity, sedentary behavior) (2). Higher percentage of sperm DNA fragmentation affects the fertilization rate and the development of the embryo and pregnancy rate.
Who should take sperm DFI tests?

items: Unexplained infertility: Normal semen analysis but difficulty conceiving.
Recurrent pregnancy loss: Two or more miscarriages.
Failed IVF/ICSI: Poor embryo development despite good sperm count.
Men over 40: Age increases risk of DNA damage.
Unhealthy lifestyle and exposure to toxic pollutants: Smoking, obesity, alcohol, heat exposure, or stress.
Varicocele: Enlarged scrotal veins linked to DNA damage.

body.text: Common methods to measure sperm DFI:

items: SCSA (Sperm Chromatin Structure Assay): Uses flow cytometry and acridine orange staining to detect DNA strand breaks
TUNEL Assay (Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP Nick End Labeling): Labels free 3′-OH DNA ends caused by fragmentation using fluorescent probes .
Comet Assay: Sperm cells are embedded in gel, lysed, and subjected to electrophoresis. Damaged DNA forms a “comet tail.”
SCD Test (Sperm Chromatin Dispersion): Sperm with intact DNA forms a halo of dispersed chromatin; fragmented DNA does not.

body.text: Rationale and Clinical Preference Although all four assays correlate reasonably well with each other and with reproductive outcomes, the Sperm Chromatin Dispersion (SCD) test is most commonly employed in clinical practice due to several practical advantages: Simplicity and accessibility, Cost-effectiveness, Reproducibility.

title: Understanding Causes, Diagnosis, and Treatment Options of Male Infertility
excerpt: Causes, diagnosis and treatment of male infertility — from varicocele and hormones to infection, genetics and lifestyle.

body.text: Introduction

Infertility is a topic of concern that affects many couples worldwide. While often associated with female factors, it’s important to recognize that male infertility contributes significantly to fertility issues. Understanding the causes, diagnosis, and treatment options for male infertility is crucial for couples seeking to start a family. In this blog article, we will delve into the various aspects of male infertility and shed light on potential solutions, including male infertility treatment.
Causes of Male Infertility:
Abnormal sperm production : Factors such as low sperm count (oligospermia) or absence of sperm (azoospermia) can significantly impact fertility.
Sperm motility issues : Poor sperm movement and swimming ability can hinder their ability to reach and fertilize the egg.
Structural abnormalities : Physical obstructions or blockages in the reproductive system, such as varicoceles, ejaculatory duct obstructions, or congenital abnormalities, can impede sperm delivery.
Hormonal imbalances : Disruptions in hormone production, particularly testosterone and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), can affect sperm production and quality.
Genetic factors : Certain genetic disorders, such as Klinefelter syndrome or Y chromosome deletions, can cause male infertility.
Diagnosis of Male Infertility :

IUI treatment in Chennai plays a vital role in enhancing fertility by significantly increasing the accessibility of sperm to the egg. Through the careful introduction of specially prepared sperm into the uterus, IUI bypasses potential obstacles and maximizes the chances of successful fertilization.
Semen analysis : A comprehensive evaluation of semen, including sperm count, motility, morphology, and other factors, is crucial to assess male fertility.
Hormonal testing : Blood tests can determine hormone levels, identifying any imbalances that may contribute to infertility.
Genetic testing : Analyzing the genetic makeup can reveal hereditary factors or abnormalities impacting fertility.
Imaging tests : Techniques like ultrasound, MRI, or a testicular biopsy may be conducted to examine the reproductive organs and detect any physical abnormalities.
Treatment Options for Male Infertility:

Lifestyle modifications : Adopting a healthy lifestyle, including regular exercise, a balanced diet, avoiding smoking and excessive alcohol consumption, and managing stress, can positively impact sperm quality.
Medications : Depending on the underlying cause, certain medications may be prescribed to address hormonal imbalances or stimulate sperm production.
Surgical interventions : Procedures such as varicocele repair or vasectomy reversal can help restore fertility in specific cases.
Assisted reproductive techniques : Methods such as intrauterine insemination (IUI) or in vitro fertilization (IVF) may be utilized to facilitate conception by bypassing certain fertility barriers.

Sperm retrieval procedures : Techniques like testicular sperm extraction (TESE) or microdissection TESE (micro-TESE) can retrieve viable sperm directly from the testes for use in assisted reproductive procedures.
Conclusion

Male infertility is a complex issue influenced by various causes. Understanding these factors, accurate diagnosis, and the available treatment options are vital for couples facing fertility challenges. Usually the postpartum period lasts somewhere between 6 to 8 weeks. You need to utilize this time to prioritise yourself and to rebuild your strength again. Here we are going to discuss many things which can make your transition convenient and stress free.

Breast feeding: Breastfeeding your baby is very important to get the first bond with your baby. Help: Your partner should understand that your body needs a lot of attention. Put him engaged with the baby in rounds so that you get to take care of yourself.

Pregnancy places additional strain on the pelvic floor muscles. Specific exercises, such as Kegels, are integral to maintaining pelvic health and preventing issues like incontinence. At GBR Fertility Centre, we emphasize the importance of these exercises and how yoga can complement them.

title: What is Hydrosalpinx and why is it a concern?
excerpt: A fluid-filled, blocked tube can quietly reduce the chance of implantation. Why hydrosalpinx matters and how it is managed.

body.text: Introduction

When the fallopian tubes get blocked or damaged, swollen and filled with fluid, it is called Hydrosalpinx. Fallopian tubes are attached to the uterus on either side and are responsible to pick up the eggs from the ovary every month and this is where the sperm meets the egg.

The fertilization happens in these tubes and the embryo travels across the fallopian tubes and enters the uterus where it gets attached to the wall and develops into a baby. This process is not possible when the tubes are blocked and this poses a major concern for couples who find it difficult to have a baby. This results in abnormal pregnancies with complications Eg. Ectopic pregnancy which mostly can be life threatening.
What Causes Hydrosalpinx?

Tubal disease is responsible for one third of all female factor infertility, and the prevalence of hydrosalpinx is as high as 30% in women with tubal pathology. Although in-vitro fertilization (IVF) was first developed to treat tubal infertility, it was soon observed that patients with hydrosalpinx had a poor outcome after IVF treatment.
How common is this?

Usually any damage to the tubes, infection or inflammation will result in swollen and fluid filled tubes. Other reasons like surgeries directly in the tubes, adhesions of the uterus wall or pelvis, sexually transmitted infection or other infections like TB or Chlamydia.
What are the symptoms of Hydrosalpinx?

Usually females with Hydrosalpinx go asymptomatic for a longer period till they start the process of fertility treatment or conception, Difficulty in fertilisation or infertility is the first sign of Hydrosalpinx. Few females may sometimes present with pelvic pain and unusual vaginal discharge.
These symptoms occur after a period:

items: Changes in colour or smell of the vagina

body.text: The impact of Hydrosalpinx with Fertility and IVF

Since Fallopian tubes play a vital role in the process of fertilization, blocked tubes cause an increased rate of failures with IVF procedures. Hydrosalpinx needs to be treated, disconnected by blocking or clipping and removed before starting the IVF procedures, which can increase the success rates drastically. If the Hydrosalpinx goes untreated, this condition will compromise the IVF efforts, sometime the fluid may leak into the uterus during embryo transfer or after into the uterine cavity and leads to many complications and poor outcome.
How is Hydrosalpinx ruled out?

items: Ultrasound where the sac is viewed and identified a sausage shaped larger areas
Hysterosalpingogram – This is a form of X-Ray test, where the uterus and fallopian tubes are filled with dye and are viewed and examined under X-Ray
Laparoscopy to view the fallopian tubes directly, mostly done as a confirmation test
If the Hydrosalpinx is small, the affected part can be repaired to allow normal pregnancy. In some cases removal of the affected part is made mandatory under laparoscopy.

This is a procedure called intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI). Sometimes the sperm cannot penetrate the outer layer, for a variety of reasons. The egg’s outer layer may be thick or hard to penetrate or the sperm may be unable to swim. In these cases, ICSI can be done along with in vitro fertilization (IVF) to help fertilize the egg. During ICSI, a single sperm is injected directly into the cytoplasm of the egg.

title: GBR Fertility Centre: Your Path to Parenthood
excerpt: What actually happens between your first phone call and a pregnancy test at GBR — the consultations, the tests and the plan.

body.text: Where the journey begins

Most people arrive at a fertility clinic carrying a folder of reports and a list of things they wish someone had explained sooner. You do not need either to book a first appointment. The journey starts with a conversation, not a test.

At GBR, the first consultation is scheduled for 45 minutes and both partners are invited. Nothing is decided on that day except what to investigate next. If you decide not to continue, that is a perfectly good outcome of a consultation.
Step one: the first consultation

Your consultant takes a full history — menstrual cycles, previous pregnancies and losses, surgery, medicines, family history, and how long you have been trying. For male partners, that includes past infections, injuries, occupational exposure and lifestyle factors. This conversation often reveals the direction the investigations should take.
Step two: fertility testing
We order only the tests that will change the plan. For most couples that means a small, focused set, completed within two to three weeks.

items: Semen analysis, repeated if the first result is abnormal.
Ovarian reserve testing — AMH and an antral follicle count on ultrasound.
Tubal patency, usually with an HSG or a saline sonogram.
A uterine assessment to look for polyps, fibroids or adhesions.
Blood tests such as thyroid function, prolactin and vitamin D where relevant.

body.text: Step three: the plan

When the results are in, we sit down with you and go through them in plain language: what is normal, what is not, and what it means for your chance of pregnancy. You leave with a written plan — the recommended next step, the alternatives, the realistic odds for each, and the cost before you begin.
Treatment is a ladder, not a leap. We start at the least invasive rung that can work for you and only climb when the evidence says we should.
Step four: treatment, if it is needed

items: Ovulation induction or timed intercourse for predictable ovulation problems.
IUI when sperm numbers and tubes allow a simpler first step.
IVF or ICSI when tubes are blocked, sperm quality is low, or other options have not worked.
Laparoscopy or hysteroscopy when surgery can correct the cause rather than work around it.
Donor programmes or surrogacy where they offer the safest route to a healthy pregnancy.

body.text: Some couples need one step. Some need a combination. Some need a pause. Your plan is reviewed after every cycle, and you are never committed to a package before you understand what it includes.
Step five: pregnancy and beyond

A positive test is not the end of the relationship. Early scans, medication reviews and a handover to our obstetric team are part of the same continuum of care. Because the team already knows your history, that handover is a conversation rather than a new file.
What to bring, and what it costs

Bring any previous reports, a list of current medicines and, if possible, your partner. If you have cycled elsewhere, bring the details — a second opinion is a normal part of fertility care. Costs are explained in writing at each stage, and there are no add-ons without a clinical reason.
If you are not sure whether you are ready, book a conversation anyway. The first appointment is there to answer questions, not to begin treatment.
